title: Federal Judge Strikes Down Trump's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee, Setting Up Legal Showdown
excerpt: A Boston federal court ruled the fee was an unlawful tax Congress never authorized, contradicting an earlier Washington ruling and creating a circuit split that could reach the Supreme Court.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge ruled Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee an unlawful tax, contradicting a previous ruling.
  • The fee's implementation led to only 85 payments by mid-February, severely impacting new visa petitions.
  • Nearly 75% of H-1B approvals are for workers from India, highlighting the fee's significant impact.
  • The White House plans to appeal, asserting the president's authority to restrict foreign entry.

U.S. District Court Ruling
  • U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston struck down the $100,000 supplemental fee on new H-1B visa petitions, ruling it an unlawful tax the president had no authority to impose.
  • The decision directly contradicts a December 2025 ruling by a Washington, D.C. judge who upheld the fee, creating a circuit split that could push the issue toward the Supreme Court.
  • Nearly three-quarters of H-1B approvals go to workers from India. The fee had already caused a sharp decline in new petitions, with only 85 payments made by mid-February.
  • The White House says it will appeal, arguing the president has clear authority to restrict entry of any class of foreign nationals deemed detrimental to U.S. interests.

The Ruling

A federal judge in Boston has struck down the $100,000 supplemental fee that President Donald Trump imposed on new H-1B visa petitions, concluding it amounted to an unlawful tax that Congress never authorized the executive branch to levy.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by 20 Democratic state attorneys general who challenged the fee Trump announced in September 2025. The fee dramatically raised the cost of obtaining H-1B visas, which previously ran between $2,000 and $5,000 depending on employer size and other factors.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called."

— U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin

The Trump administration had argued the fee was a lawful monetary penalty authorized under federal immigration law, which gives the president power to restrict entry of foreign nationals he deems "detrimental to the interests of the United States." Sorokin rejected that framing entirely.

"Citizenship and Immigration Services had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee."

A Direct Contradiction

The ruling sets up a significant legal conflict. In December 2025, U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell in Washington, D.C. rejected a challenge by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and upheld the fee, finding it fell within the president's broad immigration powers. That case is now on appeal.

A third lawsuit was filed in San Francisco by religious groups and labor organizations, opening the possibility of divided rulings across three federal appellate circuits. Legal analysts say the contradictory outcomes make Supreme Court review increasingly likely.

Sorokin drew on the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down Trump's sweeping emergency tariffs. Under that precedent, the judge reasoned, the president similarly lacked authority to levy what was effectively a tax through immigration proclamations.

Legal Landscape of the H-1B Fee
September 2025
Trump announces $100,000 H-1B visa fee.
December 2025
D.C. judge upholds the fee in a separate ruling.
February 2026
Boston judge strikes down the fee, creating a circuit split.
September 2026
Fee scheduled to expire unless appealed.

Impact on Indian Workers

The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 for workers holding advanced degrees. Technology companies rely heavily on the program, and nearly three-quarters of all H-1B approvals go to workers from India.

The fee increase had an immediate chilling effect. Court filings revealed that by mid-February, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had received just 85 payments of the $100,000 fee. States that filed the lawsuit argued the fee was making it virtually impossible to recruit doctors, teachers and other specialized workers through the program.

The fee does not apply to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who typically make up a large share of new H-1B recipients. But employers seeking to bring workers from abroad — including many Indian IT professionals — faced costs that made H-1B sponsorship economically unviable.

What Comes Next

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said the administration is confident the ruling will be reversed on appeal. "President Trump has clear legal authority to restrict entry of any class of aliens he determines is not in America's best interests, and that is exactly what he did," she said.

The administration has pursued additional measures to restrict the H-1B program beyond the fee, including enhanced vetting of applicants and a proposed new selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers.

For Indian professionals and the companies that employ them, the legal uncertainty is likely to persist for months. The fee formally remains in effect under the D.C. ruling until September 2026, when it is scheduled to expire — unless the appellate courts or the Supreme Court intervene first.
